Empirical Research Plan  
“Does winning a close U.S. House race create a personal incumbency advantage in the next election?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD).

Why appropriate?  
• Treatment (incumbency) switches deterministically at the vote-share threshold of 50 percent.  
• Near the threshold, winners and losers are observationally similar; small random shocks tip the election.  
• Therefore, comparing outcomes for candidates barely above vs. barely below 50 percent isolates the causal effect of holding office, purged of candidate selection and district partisanship that vary smoothly with vote share.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  T_i = 1 if Democratic candidate’s vote share in election t > 50 percent  
  T_i = 0 if vote share < 50 percent  

Control group  
  Candidates with vote share just below 50 percent (losers).

Running variable  
  R_i = Democratic vote share in election t minus 50.  
  Cutoff c = 0.

Outcome variables (measured in election t+1 for the same individual)  
  Y1: Democratic candidate’s vote share (%).  
  Y2: Indicator for winning the seat.

Timing  
  Treatment occurs on election day of year t; outcomes realized 2 years later in year t+1.

Sample restriction  
  Contested races with both major-party candidates; focus on |R_i| ≤ h where h is an optimally chosen or pre-specified bandwidth (e.g., ±5 p.p. in baseline).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff  
  Expected vote share in t+1 would evolve smoothly with R_i absent the treatment.  
  Plausible because small differences in current‐cycle margin are unlikely to affect future performance except through incumbency.

A2. No precise manipulation of running variable  
  Candidates cannot perfectly sort to just above 50 percent. U.S. elections use secret ballots and many precincts; recounts are rare. Plausible.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA)  
  One candidate’s victory does not affect another close-margin candidate’s outcome two years later. Reasonable within district; spillovers across districts minimal.

A4. Consistent treatment assignment at cutoff (sharp design)  
  Everyone with vote share > 50 percent is seated; everyone below is not. Virtually true except deaths/contested results, which can be dropped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Sorting or manipulation around 50 percent (violates A2).  
  Test: McCrary density test; examine “heaping” at round numbers.  
  Mitigation: Show no discontinuity in density; exclude recount races where manipulation could occur.

T2. Differential candidate attrition (loser retires, winner dies).  
  Mitigation: Use “running again” as an intermediate outcome; conduct analysis conditional on running. Report complier (Wald) estimates; robustness excluding deaths/resignations.

T3. Time-varying district boundary changes (redistricting) correlated with close races.  
  Mitigation: Restrict to periods without redistricting; include redistricting dummies; test continuity of redistricting probability at cutoff.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)     # main RDD estimator
library(fixest)       # for covariate-adjusted robustness
library(rddensity)    # McCrary test

# ---- 1. Load & clean ----
house <- read_csv("house_elections_1946_1998.csv")

df <- house %>% 
  filter(contested == 1) %>%                   # both major parties ran
  mutate(running_var   = dem_share_t - 50,     # vote share centered
         treat         = if_else(running_var > 0, 1, 0),
         outcome_vote  = dem_share_t1,         # vote share in t+1
         outcome_win   = as.integer(dem_win_t1 == 1)) %>%
  drop_na(running_var, outcome_vote)           # make sure outcomes exist

# ---- 2. Main specification (vote share outcome) ----
# use rdrobust with MSE-optimal bandwidth
main_vote <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_vote,
                      x = df$running_var,
                      c = 0,
                      cluster = df$district_id)   # cluster by district
print(summary(main_vote))

# ---- 3. Binary outcome ----
main_win <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_win,
                     x = df$running_var,
                     c = 0,
                     cluster = df$district_id,
                     p = 1, h = 0.05)  # local linear, 5 p.p. BW
summary(main_win)

# ---- 4. McCrary density test ----
density_test <- rddensity(X = df$running_var, c = 0)
summary(density_test)

# ---- 5. Covariate balance check (placebo RDs) ----
covariates <- c("age_candidate", "years_in_district", "incumbent_quality_score")
for (v in covariates) {
  res <- rdrobust(y = df[[v]], x = df$running_var, c = 0)
  print(paste("Covariate:", v))
  print(summary(res)$coef[1,])
}

# ---- 6. Robustness: polynomial order & bandwidth sweep ----
bws <- c(0.03, 0.05, 0.07)
for (b in bws) {
  res <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_win, x = df$running_var, c = 0, h = b, p = 1)
  cat("\nBandwidth:", b, "RD estimate:", res$coef[1], "\n")
}

# ---- 7. Visual RD plot ----
rdplot(y = df$outcome_win, x = df$running_var, c = 0,
       nbins = 40, p = 1, title = "Incumbency RD Plot",
       x.label = "Democratic margin in t (%)", y.label = "P(win) in t+1")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition and prior literature suggest a sizable positive incumbency advantage.

Direction: Winning a close election should raise the probability of winning the next election.

Magnitude (baseline prior):  
• For candidates at the cutoff, expect ≈ 30–40 percentage-point jump in re-election probability (going from ~50 % to ~80–90 %).  
• For vote share outcome, anticipate ≈ 8–10 p.p. increase.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Smooth density of running variable at cutoff ………………… 1  
C2: Covariate continuity at cutoff …………………………………… 1  
C3: Correct functional form / optimal bandwidth ………………… 1  
C4: No other treatment changes exactly at cutoff ………………… 1  
C5: Robustness across bandwidths & specifications ……………… 1  

Total = 5/5 → high internal validity, subject to usual RDD caveats.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
